title: Lenten customs
hook: Friday fish, Stations, and a box for the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharistic fast: an hour of going without before communion. Your line was hungry for him. What did you find you were hungry for? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

A Friday in March. The church hall smells of fried fish, and a volunteer in an apron is handing out paper plates of cod and coleslaw. Upstairs, at seven, a small group walks slowly around the church, stopping at each of the stations on the walls. At home, on the kitchen counter, there's a little cardboard box with a slot in the top, and the coins in it rattle when someone moves it to wipe the counter. None of these things happen at Mass. They happen in halls, hallways and kitchens. In homes like these, Lent lives in the house as much as in the church. Today, Lenten customs.
screen: `FISH IN THE CHURCH HALL.` → `STATIONS AT SEVEN.` → `A BOX ON THE KITCHEN COUNTER.`

segments.voice: Start with a passage in Matthew's Gospel where Jesus speaks about three things: giving alms, praying, and fasting. He says to do all three quietly. On alms, the Douay-Rheims has him say: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Prayer, fasting, almsgiving. Each custom fits under one of them. Start with Friday fish, which belongs to fasting. Church law makes Fridays days of penance and names abstinence from meat as a Friday practice, kept with special care in Lent. Fish isn't counted as meat, so fish often lands on the Friday table, and some parishes hold fish fries. The point isn't the fish. It's the meat you went without, and the small daily reminder that Friday is the day of the cross. Next, the Stations of the Cross, which belong to prayer. On Lenten Fridays, some parishes walk the stations together, stopping at each image of Jesus's last journey, from his condemnation to the tomb. It's a prayer you do with your feet. Then the box for the poor, which belongs to almsgiving. Families keep a small box or jar through Lent, drop in what they saved by skipping a treat or eating simply, and bring it to church at the end. The savings from the fast become the alms. That's the quiet logic of Lent: the three practices feed each other. What you give up in fasting, you give away in alms, and you carry both into prayer. It works best in a kitchen, on an ordinary weekday, with nobody watching. Left hand, right hand.
screen: `PRAYER, FASTING, ALMSGIVING.` · `FRIDAY FISH, FOR THE FAST.` · `THE STATIONS, FOR PRAYER.` · `A BOX FOR THE POOR, FOR ALMS.` · then, large: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one Lenten custom to keep, whatever the season. Settle, and breathe. Look at the three. Going without something, like meat on a Friday. Walking and praying, like the Stations. Setting money aside for someone who needs it, like the box on the counter. Which one could you actually do this week, at home? Pick just one. See exactly where it would happen: which meal, which corner of the house, which jar. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, simply decide, quietly, and tell no one. The bell holds the time.
Lenten customs. Friday fish, the Stations of the Cross, and a box for the poor: fasting, prayer and almsgiving, kept at home and in the parish. Today's word.
Your line: lent at home. Today, find a jar or a box, put it somewhere you'll see it, and drop in one small thing you saved by going without. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: In Lent, Catholics abstain from meat on Fridays, and some parishes hold fish fries and pray the Stations of the Cross on Friday evenings. Some families keep a box or jar for alms at home and give what they save to the poor at the end of Lent.

original.note: Latin, the Way of the Cross: the Church's name for the Stations.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholics eat fish on Fridays because of a rule.
what it means: Fridays are days of penance; in Lent Catholics go without meat, pray the Stations, and set aside alms for the poor.
what a scholar hears: the customs map onto the three practices Jesus names in Matthew 6: almsgiving, prayer and fasting.

notes: Matthew 6:1–6, 16–18 is the Gospel of Ash Wednesday; 'read at the start of Lent' relies on that. Confirm.

Canons 1250–1251 paraphrased: all Fridays are penitential days; abstinence from meat is observed on Fridays (in the US, required on the Fridays of Lent, with other penances possible on other Fridays). The teach says 'abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent'; confirm wording for an international audience.
'Fish isn't counted as meat' and the growth of parish fish fries around it: confirm phrasing; no history or dates given.
'Some parishes' and 'some families' used for the customs. The box is kept generic and does not name any charity's program.
